questions.stem: A long paper strip is folded in half three times in a row, always in the same direction, so that it makes a stack of 8 layers. One straight cut is made across the whole stack, at a place that is not on a fold and not at an end. The strip is then unfolded. How many pieces is it in?
questions.solution: The cut goes through all 8 layers, so it cuts the strip in 8 different places. Eight cuts across a strip make 8 + 1 = 9 pieces.

solve.work: Cut meets the strip at 8 points, giving 9 pieces.

questions.stem: A tank has a rectangular base 10 cm by 20 cm and is 30 cm tall. It holds 3 litres of water (1 litre is 1000 cubic centimetres). How deep is the water, in centimetres?
questions.solution: The water has volume 3000 cubic centimetres and the base has area 10 x 20 = 200 square centimetres. The depth is 3000 / 200 = 15 cm, which is less than the 30 cm height.

questions.stem: On a normal die, the numbers on opposite faces always add up to 7. Lara stands a die on a table with the 2 on top. What is the sum of the numbers on the four faces around the sides?
questions.solution: All six faces add up to 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21. The top and bottom are opposite faces, so together they show 7. The four side faces show 21 - 7 = 14.

questions.skill: Rectangle cut at a fraction of its length
questions.stem: A rectangle is 12 cm long and 8 cm wide. A straight cut, parallel to the 8 cm sides, is made one third of the way along the 12 cm side, so it splits the rectangle into two rectangles. What is the area of the larger one, in square centimetres?
questions.solution: One third of 12 is 4, so the pieces are 4 cm by 8 cm and 8 cm by 8 cm. The larger piece has area 8 x 8 = 64 square centimetres.

solve.work: Cut at 4 cm: pieces 32 and 64; larger 64.

questions.skill: Perimeter after cutting out a corner
questions.stem: A rectangle is 10 cm long and 6 cm wide. A square with sides of 3 cm is cut out of one corner, leaving an L-shaped piece. What is the perimeter of the L-shaped piece, in centimetres?
questions.solution: Cutting out the corner removes 3 cm of the old edge on each of two sides, but the cut adds two new edges of 3 cm each. So the perimeter stays 2 x (10 + 6) = 32 cm.

solve.work: Removing a corner square keeps the perimeter: 2(10+6)=32.

questions.skill: Counting the inner block of a rectangle
questions.stem: A rectangle is made of 6 rows of 8 unit squares. All the squares along the outer edge (the first and last rows and the first and last columns) are coloured grey. How many unit squares are not grey?
questions.solution: The squares that are not grey form a block with two fewer rows and two fewer columns: 4 rows of 6 squares. That is 4 x 6 = 24 squares.

questions.skill: Cubes with exactly two painted faces
questions.stem: A big cube is built from 125 small cubes: 5 layers of 5 rows of 5 cubes. Its whole outside is painted, and then it is taken apart. How many of the small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
questions.solution: Exactly two painted faces means a cube on an edge of the big cube, but not at a corner. Each of the 12 edges has 5 - 2 = 3 such cubes. That makes 12 x 3 = 36.

questions.stem: A square has an area of 64 square centimetres. The midpoints of its sides are joined to make a second square, and the midpoints of the sides of the second square are joined to make a third square. What is the area of the third square, in square centimetres?
questions.solution: Each new square has half the area of the one before it. So the second square has area 32 and the third has area 16 square centimetres.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 20 cm long and 12 cm wide. A first cut, parallel to the 12 cm sides, cuts off a piece that is two fifths of the length. The remaining piece is cut by a second cut, parallel to the 20 cm sides, which takes off a strip one quarter of the way across the 12 cm width. There are now three pieces. What is the area of the smallest one, in square centimetres?
questions.solution: The first cut gives a piece 8 cm by 12 cm (area 96) and a square piece 12 cm by 12 cm. The strip is 12 cm by 3 cm, with area 36, and the rest of the square is 12 cm by 9 cm, with area 108. The smallest is 36.

solve.work: First piece 8x12=96; remaining 12x12 split into 3x12=36 and 9x12=108; smallest 36.

questions.skill: Volume of a stone from the rise of water
questions.stem: A rectangular box has a base 20 cm by 15 cm. It contains water 6 cm deep. A stone is lowered into the water and sinks to the bottom, completely covered. The water level rises to 9 cm. What is the volume of the stone, in cubic centimetres?
questions.solution: The rise of 3 cm over the whole base of 20 x 15 = 300 square centimetres is the volume of the stone. So the stone has volume 300 x 3 = 900 cubic centimetres.

questions.stem: The faces of a cube are numbered 1 to 6, one number on each face. The faces 1, 2 and 3 meet at one corner. The face 4 shares an edge with the faces 1 and 3, and the face 5 shares an edge with the faces 2 and 3. Which number is on the face opposite the face 6?
questions.solution: The faces 1, 2, 3 meet at a corner, so their opposite faces are 4, 5 and 6 in some order. Face 4 touches 1 and 3, so it is opposite 2. Face 5 touches 2 and 3, so it is opposite 1. That leaves 6 opposite 3.

solve.work: 1,2,3 mutually adjacent so opposite pairs map to 4,5,6; 4 opposite 2, 5 opposite 1, so 6 opposite 3.

questions.skill: Marks that coincide when cutting a rope
questions.stem: A rope is marked at every one sixth of its length and also at every one quarter of its length, measured from one end. The rope is cut at every mark. How many pieces are there?
questions.solution: The sixths give 5 marks and the quarters give 3 marks. The mark at one half is in both lists (3/6 = 2/4), so there are 5 + 3 - 1 = 7 different marks. Seven cuts make 8 pieces.

solve.work: Marks at 1/6..5/6 and 1/4,1/2,3/4; 1/2 shared, 7 distinct cuts -> 8 pieces.

questions.stem: Tom looks at a round wall clock in a mirror. In the image the 12 is still at the top, but left and right are swapped. The image looks exactly like a clock showing 9:20. What time does the clock really show?
questions.solution: In a mirror the time seen is 12:00 minus the real time. So the real time is 12:00 - 9:20 = 2:40. Check: at 2:40 the minute hand points at 8, which looks like 4 (20 minutes) in the mirror, and the hour hand, two thirds of the way from 2 to 3, looks like it is a third of the way from 9 to 10.

questions.stem: A square card lies flat on a table with a star in its top-left corner. It is turned a quarter turn clockwise 5 times, and then a quarter turn anticlockwise 2 times. Looking down at the table, in which corner is the star now?
questions.solution: Five clockwise quarter turns and two anticlockwise ones are the same as 5 - 2 = 3 quarter turns clockwise. The star moves from top-left to top-right, then bottom-right, then bottom-left.

solve.work: Net 3 clockwise = 1 anticlockwise quarter turn; top-left -> bottom-left.

questions.stem: A staircase shape is made from three rectangles, each 2 cm tall, stacked on top of each other with their left edges lined up. The bottom one is 9 cm wide, the middle one 6 cm wide and the top one 3 cm wide. What is the perimeter of the whole shape, in centimetres?
questions.solution: The horizontal parts of the boundary add up to twice the bottom width, 2 x 9 = 18, and the vertical parts add up to twice the total height, 2 x 6 = 12. The perimeter is 18 + 12 = 30 cm.

questions.skill: Area of a path round a garden
questions.stem: A rectangular garden is 14 m long and 9 m wide. A path 1 m wide runs all the way round, inside the fence and along it. What is the area of the path, in square metres?
questions.solution: The whole garden has area 14 x 9 = 126 square metres. The part inside the path is 12 m by 7 m, with area 84. So the path has area 126 - 84 = 42 square metres.

questions.skill: Water level when a solid sticks out
questions.stem: A tank has a rectangular base 30 cm by 20 cm and is very tall. Water is poured in until it is 5 cm deep. Then a solid cube with edges of 10 cm is placed on the bottom of the tank. How deep is the water now, in centimetres?
questions.solution: The water has volume 30 x 20 x 5 = 3000 cubic centimetres. If the water stays below the top of the cube (10 cm), it fills a base of 600 - 100 = 500 square centimetres around the cube, so its depth is 3000 / 500 = 6 cm. This is below 10 cm, so the cube does stick out and the assumption holds.

questions.skill: Odd number of painted faces on a big cube
questions.stem: A big cube is built from 216 small cubes: 6 layers of 6 rows of 6 cubes. Its whole outside is painted, and then it is taken apart. How many of the small cubes have an odd number of painted faces?
questions.solution: An odd number of painted faces means 3 (a corner cube) or 1 (a cube inside a face, not on an edge). There are 8 corners. Each face has 4 x 4 = 16 such cubes, so 6 x 16 = 96. In all 8 + 96 = 104.

solve.work: Odd faces: corners 8 (3 faces) + face centres 6*16=96 (1 face) = 104.

questions.skill: Folding twice and cutting a corner
questions.stem: A square sheet of paper is folded in half, and then folded in half again the other way, to make a small square with 4 layers. One corner of this small square is the centre of the sheet, and the opposite corner is a corner of the sheet. A straight cut through all the layers takes a small triangle off the corner that was a corner of the sheet. The sheet is unfolded. How many separate pieces are there?
questions.solution: The four layers have four different corners of the sheet at that point of the small square, so the cut takes off a small triangle at each of the four corners of the sheet. These are 4 separate triangles, and the rest of the sheet is still one piece. In all 5 pieces.

solve.work: The folded corner holds the 4 sheet corners, no fold there, so 4 separate triangles + the sheet = 5.

questions.skill: Turning a shaded board a quarter
questions.stem: A square board has 4 rows and 4 columns of cells. Rows are counted from the top (row 1 is the top row) and columns from the left. Five cells are shaded: row 1 column 2, row 2 column 2, row 3 column 2, row 3 column 3 and row 4 column 4. The board is turned a quarter turn clockwise, and the shading turns with it. After the turn, how many of the shaded cells are in a place that was also shaded before the turn?
questions.solution: A quarter turn clockwise sends the cell in row r and column c to row c and column 5 - r. The five shaded cells go to row 2 column 4, row 2 column 3, row 2 column 2, row 3 column 2 and row 4 column 1. Of these, row 2 column 2 and row 3 column 2 were shaded before, so the answer is 2.

questions.skill: Squares cut from a rectangle in turn
questions.stem: A rectangle is 21 cm long and 13 cm wide. The biggest possible square is cut off one end. Then the biggest possible square is cut from the rectangle that is left, and so on with each rectangle that is left, until only squares remain. How many squares are there in all?
questions.solution: The squares have sides 13 (leaving 8 by 13), 8 (leaving 8 by 5), 5 (leaving 5 by 3), 3 (leaving 3 by 2), 2 (leaving 2 by 1), and then 1 and 1. That is 7 squares; their areas 169 + 64 + 25 + 9 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 273 = 21 x 13.

questions.skill: Surface of a solid with a cross-shaped hole
questions.stem: A 3 x 3 x 3 cube is made of 27 unit cubes with edges of 1 cm. The cube in the middle of each of the six faces is taken out, and so is the cube in the very centre, so 7 cubes are removed and 20 remain. What is the area, in square centimetres, of the whole surface of the remaining solid, counting the surface inside the holes as well?
questions.solution: The 20 cubes have 20 x 6 = 120 faces. Each of the 8 corner cubes touches 3 edge cubes, which is 24 touching pairs, and no other cubes touch. Each touching pair hides 2 faces, so the surface is 120 - 2 x 24 = 72 square centimetres.

solve.work: 20 cubes x 6 = 120 faces minus 2 x 24 shared faces (each edge cube touches 2 corners) = 72.

questions.skill: Counting squares of every size in a grid
questions.stem: A rectangle is made of unit squares in 3 rows and 5 columns. How many squares of any size (1 x 1, 2 x 2 or 3 x 3) can be found in it, with their sides along the grid lines?
questions.solution: There are 3 x 5 = 15 squares of size 1 x 1. For size 2 x 2 there are 2 x 4 = 8 positions, and for size 3 x 3 there are 1 x 3 = 3 positions. In all 15 + 8 + 3 = 26.

questions.skill: Volume of a box folded from a sheet
questions.stem: A square sheet of cardboard has sides of 12 cm. A square with sides of 3 cm is cut from each of the four corners, and the four flaps that are left are folded up to make an open box with no lid. What is the volume of the box, in cubic centimetres?
questions.solution: The base of the box is a square with side 12 - 3 - 3 = 6 cm, and the box is 3 cm high. The volume is 6 x 6 x 3 = 108 cubic centimetres.

questions.skill: Where the cuts fall after folding a strip
questions.stem: A paper strip is 80 cm long. It is folded in half three times in a row, always in the same direction, to make a stack of 8 layers, each 10 cm long. One straight cut is made across the whole stack at a place 3 cm from one end of the stack. The strip is unfolded and is in pieces. How long, in centimetres, is the longest piece?
questions.solution: The folds are at 10, 20, ..., 70 cm, and the layers lie alternately forwards and backwards. So the cuts are at 3, 17, 23, 37, 43, 57, 63 and 77 cm from one end. The pieces are 3, 14, 6, 14, 6, 14, 6, 14 and 3 cm long, and the longest is 14 cm.

solve.work: Zigzag layers: cuts at 3,17,23,37,...,77 -> pieces 3,14,6,...,14,3 (or 7,6,14,... from other end); longest 14.

questions.skill: Least perimeter of ten joined squares
questions.stem: Ten unit squares, each with sides of 1 cm, are joined side to side (whole sides touching) into one piece. What is the smallest possible perimeter of the piece, in centimetres?
questions.solution: A shape that fits inside a rectangle of w by h squares has perimeter at least 2(w + h). Ten squares do not fit in 3 x 3 (only 9), so w + h is at least 7 and the perimeter is at least 14. A 3 by 4 rectangle with two corner squares removed has perimeter exactly 14.

questions.stem: A drawer holds many red, blue and green socks, all mixed up. In the dark, how many socks must you take out to be sure of having two of the same colour?
questions.solution: In the worst case the first three socks have three different colours. The fourth sock must match one of them, so 4 socks are enough and 3 are not.

questions.skill: Day of the week after many days
questions.stem: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from today?
questions.solution: Days of the week repeat every 7 days. 100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so the day is 2 days after Wednesday, which is Friday.

questions.stem: Two players take turns taking 1, 2, 3 or 4 sticks from a pile. Whoever takes the last stick wins. The pile has 17 sticks and Dana moves first. How many sticks should Dana take first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Dana wants to leave a multiple of 5, because whatever the other player takes (1 to 4), Dana can then take enough to make the total taken in that round 5. So she takes 2 and leaves 15, and keeps leaving multiples of 5 until she takes the last stick.

questions.skill: Counting walks that visit every place once
questions.stem: Five camps P, Q, R, S and T are joined by 6 paths: P-Q, Q-R, R-S, S-T, T-P and Q-S. No other two camps are joined. A hiker starts at P and visits every camp exactly once, walking only along paths. How many different routes are there?
questions.solution: Starting at P the hiker can go to Q or to T. Going to Q: P-Q-R-S-T works, and P-Q-S-T leaves out R, while P-Q-S-R leaves out T. Going to T: P-T-S-R-Q and P-T-S-Q-R both work. So there are 3 routes.

solve.work: P-Q-R-S-T, P-T-S-R-Q, P-T-S-Q-R; P-Q-S branches dead-end.

questions.stem: A round pizza is cut into three slices by three cuts from the centre to the edge, so each slice touches both of the others along a cut. The slices are coloured so that slices that touch have different colours. What is the smallest number of colours needed?
questions.solution: Each slice touches the other two, so all three slices need different colours. Three colours are needed, and three are enough.

solve.work: Three mutually touching slices need 3 colours.

questions.stem: A snail climbs a wall that is 10 m high. Each day it climbs 3 m up, and each night it slips 1 m back down. It stops as soon as it reaches the top. On which day does it reach the top?
questions.solution: Each full day and night the snail gains 2 m. After 4 days and nights it is at 8 m. On day 5 it climbs 3 m and reaches 11 m, so it is at the top on day 5. On day 4 it only reached 9 m.

solve.work: Starts day 5 at 8 m, climbs to the top; day 4 only reaches 9 m.

questions.stem: Four cards lie in a row and show 3, 4, 1, 2 in this order. In one move you may swap two cards that are next to each other. What is the smallest number of moves needed to put the cards in the order 1, 2, 3, 4?
questions.solution: Each of the cards 1 and 2 has to pass both of the cards 3 and 4, and each swap of neighbours can fix only one such pair. There are 2 x 2 = 4 pairs that are the wrong way round, so at least 4 moves are needed. For example: 3 4 1 2, 3 1 4 2, 1 3 4 2, 1 3 2 4, 1 2 3 4.

solve.work: Inversions of 3,4,1,2 = 4; adjacent swaps remove one each.

questions.stem: A night train leaves at 22:40 and the journey takes 3 hours 35 minutes. At what time does it arrive, on the 24-hour clock? (The new day starts at 00:00.)
questions.solution: From 22:40, 1 hour 20 minutes brings us to midnight, 00:00. The rest of the journey is 3 hours 35 minutes - 1 hour 20 minutes = 2 hours 15 minutes. So the train arrives at 02:15.

questions.stem: There are 30 children in a class. Whatever their birthdays are, there is a month in which at least $n$ of them have a birthday. What is the largest value of $n$ for which this is always true?
questions.solution: There are 12 months. If every month had at most 2 birthdays there would be at most 24 children, but there are 30. So some month has at least 3. And 4 is not always true, since each month could have 2 or 3 children (for example, 6 months with 3 and 6 months with 2).

solve.work: ceil(30/12)=3; 6 months of 2 and 6 of 3 shows 4 not forced.

questions.stem: Mia thinks of a number. She multiplies it by 3, subtracts 4, and then halves the result. She gets 10. What number did Mia think of?
questions.solution: Undo the steps in reverse order. Before halving the number was 10 x 2 = 20. Before subtracting 4 it was 24. Before multiplying by 3 it was 24 / 3 = 8.

questions.skill: Game where taking the last loses
questions.stem: Two players take turns taking 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 coins from a pile of 23 coins. Whoever takes the last coin LOSES. Eli goes first. How many coins should he take first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Eli wants to leave the other player with 1 more than a multiple of 6: then, whatever she takes, Eli can bring the total taken in that round to 6, and in the end she is left with the last coin. 23 - 4 = 19 = 3 x 6 + 1, so Eli takes 4.

questions.skill: Worst case for four of a colour
questions.stem: A bag has 7 red, 5 blue, 4 green and 3 yellow balls, all alike except for colour. You take balls without looking. How many balls must you take to be sure of having at least 4 balls of the same colour?
questions.solution: In the worst case you hold 3 red, 3 blue, 3 green and all 3 yellow balls, which is 12 balls and no colour has 4. The next ball is red, blue or green and gives 4 of one colour. So 13 balls are needed.

solve.work: Worst case 3 of each of 4 colours = 12, then one more.

questions.stem: Eight books stand in a row on a shelf in the order 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. In one move you may swap any two books, not only neighbours. What is the smallest number of moves needed to put them in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8?
questions.solution: Swapping the books 8 and 1, then 7 and 2, then 6 and 3, then 5 and 4 puts them in order, so 4 moves are enough. Each move can put at most 2 books in their right places, and all 8 books are in the wrong places, so at least 8 / 2 = 4 moves are needed.

questions.stem: Five camps A, B, C, D and E are joined by 7 paths: A-B, A-C, B-C, B-D, C-D, C-E and D-E. No other two camps are joined. A hiker starts at A and visits every camp exactly once, walking only along paths. How many different routes are there?
questions.solution: List the routes: ABCDE, ABCED, ABDCE, ABDEC, ACBDE and ACEDB. A route that begins A-C-D fails, because B and E are left and they are not joined. So there are 6 routes.

solve.work: From A-B: 4 paths; from A-C: A-C-B-D-E, A-C-E-D-B; total 6.

questions.skill: Colouring a ring around a centre
questions.stem: A round mat has a circle in the centre and five curved pieces around it, forming a ring. Each of the five pieces touches the central circle and the two pieces next to it in the ring, and touches nothing else. Regions that touch must have different colours. What is the smallest number of colours needed?
questions.solution: The central circle touches all five pieces, so it needs a colour that none of them use. The five pieces form a ring with an odd number of pieces, so two colours are not enough for them (they would have to alternate). They need 3 colours, and with the centre that makes 4. Four colours work.

solve.work: Odd ring of 5 needs 3, centre touches all: 4.

questions.stem: Start with the number 1. Each step: if the number is even, halve it; if it is odd, add 5. The sequence begins 1, 6, 3, 8, ... What is the 21st number in the sequence?
questions.solution: Continuing: 1, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, 6, ... so the numbers repeat in a cycle of length 6. The 21st number is 20 steps after the first, and 20 = 3 x 6 + 2, so it is the same as the 3rd number, which is 3.

questions.skill: Dates and days of the week
questions.stem: In a certain month, exactly three of the Tuesdays fall on even-numbered dates. On what day of the week is the 25th of that month?
questions.solution: A month has 4 or 5 Tuesdays. Only if the Tuesdays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th are three of them even (2, 16 and 30); any other month has at most 2 even Tuesdays. So the 23rd is a Tuesday and the 25th is two days later, a Thursday.

solve.work: Only Tuesdays 2,9,16,23,30 give three even dates; 25th is Thursday.

questions.stem: A faulty clock loses 5 minutes in every real hour, so it shows only 55 minutes in each real hour. It was set right at 8:00 in the morning. Later, the faulty clock shows 1:30 in the afternoon. What is the real time?
questions.solution: The clock shows 5 hours 30 minutes = 330 minutes since 8:00. It shows 55 minutes for each real hour, so the real time that has passed is 330 / 55 = 6 hours. The real time is 8:00 + 6 hours = 2:00 in the afternoon.

solve.work: Clock shows 5.5 h = 0.9167 real; real elapsed 5.5*60/55=6 h -> 2:00 pm.

questions.stem: A shop has some apples. The first customer buys half of the apples and one more apple. The second customer buys half of the apples that are left and one more. The third customer does the same, buying half of what is then left and one more, and after that no apples are left. How many apples did the shop have at the start?
questions.solution: Work backwards. Before the third customer there were 2 apples (half of 2 is 1, plus 1 more is 2). Before the second, x apples became x / 2 - 1 = 2 left, so x = 6. Before the first, x / 2 - 1 = 6 gives x = 14.

questions.skill: Pigeonhole with pairs that add up
questions.stem: Cards numbered 1 to 30 lie face down. How many cards must you turn over to be sure that two of them add up to 31?
questions.solution: The numbers form 15 pairs that add to 31: 1 and 30, 2 and 29, up to 15 and 16. With 15 cards you could take one from each pair and have no two adding to 31. The 16th card must complete a pair. So 16 cards are needed.

solve.work: 15 pairs summing to 31; 16 cards forces a pair.

questions.stem: Ali, Bea and Cy have 24 marbles in all. First Ali gives Bea and Cy as many marbles as each of them already has. Then Bea gives Ali and Cy as many as each of them now has. Then Cy gives Ali and Bea as many as each of them now has. At the end all three have 8 marbles. How many marbles did Ali have at the start?
questions.solution: Work backwards. Before Cy's gift, Ali and Bea had half of 8, that is 4 each, and Cy had 24 - 8 = 16. Before Bea's gift, Ali and Cy had 2 and 8, and Bea had 24 - 10 = 14. Before Ali's gift, Bea and Cy had 7 and 4, and Ali had 24 - 11 = 13.

questions.skill: Winning strategy by keeping heaps equal
questions.stem: Two heaps have 7 stones and 12 stones. Two players take turns; each turn a player takes any number of stones (at least one) from ONE heap. Whoever takes the last stone wins. You move first and want to be sure of winning. How many stones do you take from the heap of 12?
questions.solution: Make the heaps equal: take 5 from the heap of 12, so both have 7. Then whatever the opponent takes from one heap, copy it from the other. You can always do this, so you take the last stone. Taking any other number leaves unequal heaps, and the opponent can use the same plan.

questions.skill: Winning positions in a take-away game
questions.stem: A pile has 25 stones. Two players take turns taking 1, 3 or 4 stones (never 2). Whoever takes the last stone wins. Sam moves first and plays so as to be sure of winning. How many stones are left in the pile after Sam's first move?
questions.solution: Work up from small piles. A player to move with 0, 2, 7, 9, 14, 16, 21 or 23 stones left loses (every move leaves a pile from which the next player can win), and the pattern repeats every 7. From 25 the allowed moves leave 24, 22 or 21, and only 21 is a losing pile for the opponent. So 21 stones are left.

solve.work: P-positions n mod 7 in {0,2}; 25-4=21 is the only such move.

questions.stem: An ant walks along the edges of a cube. It starts at a corner S, visits each of the 8 corners exactly once, and finishes at the corner T that is opposite S (no face of the cube contains both S and T). How many different routes can the ant take?
questions.solution: Number the corners by three coordinates of 0 and 1, with S = 000 and T = 111. The ant must change one coordinate at each step. Listing the routes that visit all 8 corners and end at 111 gives 6, namely three choices of the first step, each with 2 ways to continue.

solve.work: Fix first edge (3 ways), second (2 ways), then forced: 6.

questions.skill: Colouring a row with matching ends
questions.stem: A row of 5 squares is coloured with red, blue and green so that squares next to each other have different colours, and the first and last squares have the same colour. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.solution: The ends have the same colour, so think of the row as a ring of 4 squares. Choose the colour of the first square in 3 ways. Colour squares 2 and 3, each different from the one before, and then square 4 must differ from square 3 and from the first colour. Squares 2 and 4 each differ from the first colour, 2 ways each. If they match (2 ways), square 3 has 2 choices, giving 4. If they differ (2 ways), square 3 must be the first colour, giving 2. That is 6 for each first colour, so 3 x 6 = 18.

solve.work: Closed walks of length 4 on K3: 2^4+1+1=18.

questions.stem: How many numbers must you choose from the numbers 1 to 20 to be sure that one of the chosen numbers divides another chosen number?
questions.solution: Write every number as an odd number times a power of 2. There are only 10 odd numbers up to 20, so among 11 chosen numbers two have the same odd part, and the smaller one divides the larger. With 10 numbers it can fail: 11, 12, ..., 20 has no number dividing another.

solve.work: 11..20 is an antichain of 10; 11 chosen forces a divisor pair (odd-part chains).

questions.skill: A repeated process on a pile of cards
questions.stem: Twenty cards numbered 1 to 20 are in a pile, with 1 on top, then 2, and so on, down to 20 at the bottom. Repeat this: move the top card to the bottom of the pile, then throw away the card that is now on top. Continue until only one card is left. What is the number on that card?
questions.solution: The first round throws away 2, 4, ..., 20 and leaves 1, 3, ..., 19 with 1 on top. The next round throws away 3, 7, 11, 15 and 19, leaving 1, 5, 9, 13, 17. Then 5, 13, 1 and 17 are thrown away in turn, and 9 is left.

questions.stem: On a round clock the hour hand and the minute hand sometimes point in exactly the same direction. How many times does this happen from just after 12:00 noon up to and including 6:00 p.m.?
questions.solution: The minute hand catches up with the hour hand once every 12/11 of an hour, about 65.45 minutes. The overlaps are at about 1:05, 2:11, 3:16, 4:22 and 5:27, and the next one is after 6:00. So there are 5.

solve.work: Coincide at 12k/11 h, k=1..5 within 6 h; at 6:00 opposite.

questions.stem: A frog sits at 0 on a number line. Each jump takes it either 5 steps to the right or 3 steps to the left. What is the smallest number of jumps with which it can land on 1?
questions.solution: With a jumps right and b jumps left the frog is at 5a - 3b. With 1 or 2 jumps the frog can only be at 5, -3, 10, 2 or -6. With n jumps in all the position is 5a - 3(n - a) = 8a - 3n, so for 3 jumps it would need 8a = 10 and for 4 jumps 8a = 13, which are impossible. With 5 jumps, 8a - 15 = 1 gives a = 2: for example 5, 2, 7, 4, 1 uses two jumps right and three left. So 5.

questions.stem: You have a 5-litre jug and a 3-litre jug with no markings, and a tap. A move is one of these: fill a jug from the tap; empty a jug; or pour from one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full. What is the smallest number of moves to get exactly 4 litres in one of the jugs?
questions.solution: Fill the 5-litre jug (5, 0). Pour into the 3-litre jug (2, 3). Empty the 3-litre jug (2, 0). Pour the 2 litres across (0, 2). Fill the 5-litre jug (5, 2). Pour into the 3-litre jug until it is full, which takes 1 litre (4, 3). That is 6 moves, and a search of all the possibilities shows that fewer is not possible.

solve.work: BFS: fill5, 5->3, empty3, 5->3, fill5, 5->3 leaves 4; no 5-move solution.
